title: Tool Calling and MCP Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Night-before revision notes on defining tools with JSON schemas, running the tool call loop, getting structured outputs, handling tool errors, and MCP basics.

chapters.title: Tool Calling Mental Model
points: Definition: a tool is a function the model can ask for by name with JSON arguments; the model never executes anything, your code does
Three parts of a tool definition: name, description, input JSON schema (the description is the prompt that tells the model when to use it)
Mechanism: you send messages plus tool definitions, the model replies with a tool call (name, id, arguments) instead of text, you run it and send the result back
Stop signal: the response says it wants tools (e.g. stop_reason tool_use or finish_reason tool_calls); a plain end_turn/stop means a final answer
Interview Point: Who executes a tool call, the model or your app? What does the model actually output when it calls a tool? How does your code know the model wants a tool?

chapters.title: Defining Tools and JSON Schemas
points: Schema basics: type object, properties, required array, and per-field type, description, enum, minimum/maximum, items for arrays
Descriptions drive tool choice: state what the tool does, when to use it, when not to, and the format of each argument
Narrow schemas beat free text: use enum for fixed choices, add additionalProperties false, and keep parameters flat
Example: get_weather with location (string, required) and unit (enum celsius/fahrenheit); the model returns {"location":"Pune","unit":"celsius"}

Mistake: vague names like do_action, listing too many overlapping tools, or marking optional fields required (the model then invents values); the schema is a hint, so always validate arguments server side
Interview Point: Why validate arguments if a schema exists? How do you stop the model picking the wrong tool? What belongs in a tool description?

chapters.title: The Tool Call Loop
points: Loop: call model, check for tool calls, run each, append the assistant message and a tool result message, call the model again, repeat until a plain answer
Match each result to its call by id (tool_use_id or tool_call_id); results must follow the assistant message that made the calls
Parallel tool calls: one response can hold several independent calls; run them concurrently and return all results together
Example skeleton: while True: resp = model(messages, tools); if no tool calls: break; for c in calls: messages.append(result(c.id, run(c))); put a max_turns cap on the loop

Mistake: no iteration cap (runaway loops and cost), dropping the assistant tool-call message from history, or returning a result with a mismatched id; tool_choice auto lets the model decide, forced/any makes it call a tool, none disables tools
Interview Point: How do you prevent infinite tool loops? How do parallel tool calls work? What goes wrong if tool results are not tied to call ids?

chapters.title: Structured Outputs and Error Handling
points: Structured output means the reply conforms to your JSON schema; either use native schema-constrained output or define a tool whose input schema is the shape you want and force it with tool_choice
Prompting for JSON is the weakest option (can add prose or break syntax); schema-constrained decoding guarantees valid JSON, but still validate values and handle refusals or truncation by max_tokens
Tool errors go back to the model as the tool result with an error flag (e.g. is_error true) and a clear message, so the model can retry, fix arguments or explain
Example: on validation failure return {"error":"unit must be celsius or fahrenheit"}; the model corrects the call; retry limited times, then fail gracefully

Mistake: raising exceptions that crash the loop, returning raw stack traces, retrying forever, or retrying non-idempotent tools (payments, emails) without safeguards; add timeouts and permission checks for destructive tools
Interview Point: How do you get guaranteed JSON from a model? What should a tool return when it fails? Why must side-effecting tools be idempotent or confirmed?

chapters.title: MCP Basics
points: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data; a host app runs MCP clients that each connect to one MCP server
A server exposes three primitives: tools (model-invoked actions), resources (readable data), prompts (reusable templates); messages use JSON-RPC 2.0
Transports: stdio for local servers launched as subprocesses, streamable HTTP for remote servers; the client lists tools with tools/list and invokes with tools/call

MCP vs hand-written function calling: MCP standardizes discovery and calling so one server works across many apps, while plain function calling needs custom glue per app; both use the same JSON schema tool definitions underneath

Mistake: trusting third-party servers blindly (prompt injection through tool output and over-broad permissions), exposing too many tools and bloating context, or logging to stdout on stdio servers (corrupts the protocol; use stderr)
Interview Point: What problem does MCP solve? Name the three MCP primitives. How do stdio and HTTP transports differ, and what are the security risks?

chapters.title: Tool Calling Cheat Sheet
points: Loop: model call, tool call detected, execute in your code, return result by id, repeat until a plain answer; always cap turns
Tool definition: name, clear description, JSON schema with types, enums, required and additionalProperties false; validate on the server
Structured output: schema-constrained output or a forced tool; still validate values and check for refusal or truncation
Errors: return them as flagged tool results with short actionable messages; limit retries; never auto-retry non-idempotent actions
Interview Point: Walk through a full tool call round trip. Function calling vs MCP? How do you make a tool-using agent safe and reliable?
